body.p: In the Final Office Action mailed on February 15, 2023, claims 1-13 are pending in the application; Claims 1-7 and 11-12 are withdrawn; Claims 8-10 and 13 stand rejected. Claims 8 and 13 are amended.
As set forth herein, reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections and objections of the claims is respectfully requested.

In the Office Action the Examiner stated that the "wherein" clause could also be interpreted that the claimed value is a numerical lung score that is compared to threshold values, and these threshold values are expressed as a scaled lung score that is defined as corresponding to respiratory conditions indicating the health status of the animals respiratory condition.
The Examiner's statement is what is intended to be claimed. Therefore, claims 8 and 13 are amended to clarify the claimed subject matter in this regard.

Claims 8-10 and 13 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over US Patent Publication No. 2006/0201432 (hereinafter referred as Pratt) in view of US Patent Publication No. 2007/0106179 (hereinafter referred as Bagha) further in view of US Patent Publication No. 2004/0236241) (hereinafter referred as Murphy). The Applicant respectfully traverses this rejection.

As mentioned in the comment on the Examiner's Response to Arguments, the scaled lung score is obtained from the calculated numerical lung score that is compared to known respiratory conditions. The scaled lung score then provides an indication of the health status of the animal. As set forth in the description, e.g., at pages 9 and 10, the preferred embodiment presented there provides scaled lung scores in the form of whole numbers ranging from 1 to 9. These scaled lung scores provide a caregiver with a simple yet reliable indication of the health status of the animal.

It is submitted that the combined teachings of the cited references do not disclose the subject matter of the aforementioned wherein clause considering the Examiner's comment on what is understood to be more clear language to distinguish over the references.

The Examiner continues to rely upon Murphy at [0081] to assert this paragraph teaches the claimed scaled lung scores. The paragraph [0081] in Murphy does not describe anything relating to the characterization of lung sounds to determine a health status but rather, this paragraph simply explains how discrete sound artifacts (i.e. noise) is distinguished from "adventitious" sounds (i.e. the targeted sounds from the respiration of the animal). An example slope threshold constant is identified in Murphy (.015) in which the median of the preliminary threshold trace is multiplied by this constant. The resulting value is then added to the preliminary threshold trace to form a slope threshold trace. Next, following the process described with respect to Figs. 8 and 9A and 9B (see [0082-0090]), it is clear that the identification of noise is necessary to obtain measurable sound data from the animal's respiration as opposed to a mixed signal that includes both noise and respiration sounds. The scaling factor mentioned in Murphy at [0081] is not a health status indicator. The scaling factor is applied to the data in order to identify the portions that correspond to a respiratory condition (adventitious sound detection), but the scaling factor alone does not provide the respiratory condition. The scaling factor is not explained but is assumed to be some mathematical coefficient or value that is combined with the data. Without the data, the scaling factor would presumably be meaningless.

While Murphy may indicate a health status of an animal (e.g., see [0117]), the logic and methodology in Murphy does not provide a scaled lung score. The process of separating undesirable noise from targeted sounds of respiration in Murphy cannot be deemed equivalent to the subject matter of the claimed wherein clause. With respect to [0117] in Murphy, to obtain a probable diagnosis, Murphy discloses that a sound detection program is employed that may be based on a neural network module such as a programming tool from a statistical classification source. The program interacts with a training database to derive the proposed diagnosis. The training database includes data corresponding to the ratio of inspiration to expiration, the numbers and locations of course, medium and fine crackles and wheezes etc. Alternatively, Murphy recites that the program may utilize a multiple logistic regression model to arrive at a proposed diagnosis. The present invention incorporates the claimed algorithm that utilizes selected frequencies of the auscultated sounds. Murphy uses a statistical classification method or a logistic regression model but does not disclose any algorithm that utilizes selected frequencies as claimed. Pratt and Bahga fail to cure the deficiencies in Murphy. Therefore, this rejection should be reconsidered and withdrawn.
Based on the foregoing, Applicant believes all pending claims are in condition for allowance and such disposition is respectfully requested.
